knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

#Problem 1(a)

```{r}
set.seed(123)
#function that calculates the three estimators

variance_estimators <- function(x) {


n <- length(x)

var_n <- sum((x-mean(x))^2)/n
var_n_minus_1 <- var(x)
sample_sd <- sd(x)

return(c(
var_n = var_n,
var_n_minus_1 = var_n_minus_1,
sample_sd = sample_sd
))
}

#Simulate a sample of 10 observations from N(0,2)

x <- rnorm(10, mean = 0, sd = 2)

#Check the function
variance_estimators(x)

```

#Problem 1(b)

```{r}
reps <- 1000
n <- 5
true_var <- 4

# 1000 samples of 5 observations from the population 
# and apply your function to each.

sim <- replicate(reps, variance_estimators(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 2)))

# Store the results in a data frame with one row per sample

sim_df <- as.data.frame(t(sim))

# Check the data frame

head(sim_df)

# Calculate the mean of each estimator

estimator_means <- colMeans(sim_df)
estimator_means

# Plot the sampling distributions
# of the two variance estimators

hist(
sim_df$var_n,
breaks = 30,
xlim = range(
c(sim_df$var_n, sim_df$var_n_minus_1)
),

xlab = "Variance Estimate",
main = "Sampling Distributions of Variance Estimators"
)

hist(
sim_df$var_n_minus_1,
breaks = 30,
add = TRUE
)

# true variance
abline(
v = true_var,
lwd = 3)

# the mean of the divide-by-n estimator
abline(
v = estimator_means["var_n"],
lty = 2)

# the mean of the divide-by-(n-1) estimator
abline(
v = estimator_means["var_n_minus_1"],
lty = 3
)

```
The divide_by_n variance estimator is downward biased. Across the 1000 simulations, its mean estimate was 3.197351, which is below the true variance of 4. In contrast, the divide_by_n-1 estimator had a mean estimate of 3.996689, which is very close to the true variance.

# Problem 1(c)

```{r}
sample_sizes <- c(3, 5, 10, 30, 100)

bias_var_n <- numeric(length(sample_sizes))
bias_var_n_minus_1 <- numeric(length(sample_sizes))

for (i in 1: length(sample_sizes)) {
n <- sample_sizes[i]
sim <- replicate(
reps,
variance_estimators(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 2))
)

sim_df <- as.data.frame(t(sim))

bias_var_n[i] <- mean(sim_df$var_n) - true_var

bias_var_n_minus_1[i] <- mean(sim_df$var_n_minus_1) - true_var}

# Show the estimated bias

bias_var_n
bias_var_n_minus_1

# Plot estimated bias against sample size

plot(
sample_sizes,
bias_var_n,
type = "b",
xlab = "Sample size (n)",
ylab = "Estimated bias",
main = "Estimated bias by Sample size"
)


lines(
sample_sizes,
bias_var_n_minus_1,
type = "b",
lty = 2
)

abline(
h = 0, lty = 3)
```

# Problem 1(d)

```{r}
sample_sizes <- c(3, 5, 10, 30, 100)
reps <- 1000
true_sd <- 2

bias_sd <- numeric(length(sample_sizes))

for (i in 1: length(sample_sizes)) {

n <- sample_sizes[i]
sim <- replicate(
reps,
variance_estimators(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd =2))
)

sim_df <- as.data.frame(t(sim))
bias_sd [i] <- mean(sim_df$sample_sd) - 2}

# The estimated bias for each sample size

sd_bias_results <- data.frame(
n = sample_sizes,
bias_sd = bias_sd)


# Results

sd_bias_results

```
The sample standard deviation s is downward biased as an estimator of sigma = 2. 
However, the magnitude of the bias becomes smaller as the sample size increases and approaches zero for larger samples.


# Problem 1(e)

```{r}
n <- 5

sim_e <- replicate(
reps,
variance_estimators(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 2)))

sim_e_df <- as.data.frame(t(sim_e))

# Standard deviation of the 1000 estimates

sd_var_n <- sd(sim_e_df$var_n)
sd_var_n_minus_1 <- sd(sim_e_df$var_n_minus_1)

sd_var_n
sd_var_n_minus_1

```
At n = 5, the sd of the 1000 estimates from the divide_by_n variance estimator is less variable.
However, lower variability does not automatically make it the better estimator because the divide_by_n estimator is downward biased. The divide_by_n-1 estimator has greater variability but is unbiased for the population variance. Thus, variability alone is not sufficient for evaluating an estimator.
